nameStory: Henbit gets its quirky name because chickens and other barnyard birds love to nibble on this little plant - "hen" plus "bit" for what they bite! The "deadnettle" part comes from its resemblance to stinging nettles, but unlike true nettles, this plant won't sting you at all - it's "dead" to the touch.
description: Henbit deadnettle is a charming little winter annual that pops up in gardens, lawns, and disturbed soil throughout New England. This low-growing member of the mint family reaches just 4-10 inches tall, forming small patches of heart-shaped leaves topped with tiny purple flowers. It's one of our earliest spring bloomers, often flowering while snow still lingers in shady spots. Despite being in the mint family, it has a square stem like its relatives but lacks the strong minty scent.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Upper leaves clasp the stem completely like little cups, while lower leaves have stalks - this stem-clasping feature is unique and diagnostic

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny purple-pink flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints, each flower shaped like a tiny snapdragon with a hooded upper lip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, sprawling patches rarely taller than your hand, with multiple branching stems that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges feel soft and slightly wrinkled, like fine velvet with rounded teeth along the margins

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers have no scent but often appear in early spring when few other plants are blooming, making them easy to spot

habitat: Look for henbit in disturbed soils like garden beds, lawn edges, vacant lots, and along pathways throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soil but adapts to various conditions from full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it mixed with other early spring weeds in cultivated areas and waste places.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time with clusters of purple flowers most visible, making identification easiest when few other plants are flowering.
seasonality.summer: Often dies back in hot weather, though may persist in cool, moist spots with reduced flowering and smaller leaves.
seasonality.fall: Seeds germinate to form new rosettes of leaves that will overwinter, appearing as small patches of heart-shaped leaves.
seasonality.winter: Persists as low rosettes of leaves under snow, often staying somewhat green and ready to bolt into flower at first spring thaw.

funFact: Henbit is one of nature's ultimate early risers - it can actually photosynthesize and grow under snow, using the insulating snow cover like a greenhouse to get a head start on spring growth while other plants are still dormant!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red deadnettle, but henbit's upper leaves clasp the stem completely (like little cups) while red deadnettle's leaves all have stalks. Memory trick: "Henbit hugs" - the leaves hug the stem without stalks.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - "deadnettle" doesn't mean this plant is dead or dying! It's called "dead" because unlike true stinging nettles, these plants won't sting you. All deadnettles are perfectly safe to touch and are actually in the mint family, not related to stinging nettles at all.
compareHints: Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants. Yellow archangel has yellow flowers and is quite rare in New England, making henbit's purple flowers and tiny size distinctive in early spring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color.

Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers.
Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves.
Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones.
White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit.
